reason: The nucleus contains opened DNA and nearby enzymes, while the nucleotides provide the building blocks needed to copy it.
expectation: The nucleotides will be used to copy the genome in the nucleus.

effect: The genome is copied, with sister chromatids still joined; the cell-growth and spindle goals remain.
reaction: The distinction between copying the whole genome and making proteins is useful.
reason: The duplicated centrosomes organize the spindle, and tubulin and motor proteins are its apparent components.
expectation: These components will form a chromosome-separating spindle.

effect: The spindle is built, and producing two daughter stem cells is now a goal; cell growth remains unfinished.
reaction: The spindle illustration makes clear that the chromosomes have not yet separated.
reason: Phospholipids can supply the additional membrane needed as the living cell grows.
expectation: The cell will add phospholipids to its surface as part of growth.

effect: The living stem cell has no available combination as the first object, so I need another route to cell growth.
reaction: I was surprised that the apparent membrane-growth pair did not work.
reason: Phospholipids are still a plausible material for surface growth, so checking their available partners should clarify the route.
expectation: The compatibility report will show how phospholipids can contribute to growth.

effect: Phospholipids and new proteins formed membrane vesicles, suggesting an intermediate step toward surface growth.
reaction: The vesicle intermediate explains why my direct attempt did not work.
reason: The vesicles could fuse with the living cell's membrane to expand its surface.
expectation: The vesicles will contribute membrane to the growing cell.

effect: The vesicles enlarged the cell body, completing the growth goal; the copied genome and spindle still need to be brought together for division.
reaction: The continuous larger membrane makes the vesicles' role clearer.
reason: The spindle must engage the copied chromosomes to separate them into daughter cells.
expectation: The spindle will engage the copied chromosomes and help separate the sister chromatids.

effect: The spindle separated the copied chromosomes into matching sets, but the cell still has one shared cytoplasm.
reaction: The distinction between chromosome separation and cell division is clear.
reason: Cortical actin and myosin are positioned beneath the membrane and could divide the enlarged cell body.
expectation: Actin and myosin will help constrict the cell body during division.

effect: The separated chromosome sets are now enclosed in two daughter nuclei within one enlarged cell; cytoplasm division remains.
reaction: The compatibility feedback clarified that the nuclei form before the cell splits.
reason: Actin and myosin beneath the membrane can constrict the cell containing the two daughter nuclei.

choice.combine: Stem cell with two daughter nuclei

expectation: The cell will constrict and divide into two daughter stem cells.

effect: Actin and myosin completed the division, producing two unspecialized daughter stem cells with complete nuclear genomes; all chapter goals are complete.
reaction: The final picture ties chromosome separation and cytoplasmic division together clearly.

mostWorthwhile.text: Separating the copied chromosomes with the spindle was most worthwhile: the result distinguished distributing sister chromatids from actually splitting the cell.

leastWorthwhile.text: The failed direct attempt to add phospholipids to the cell was the least informative on its own; inspecting the phospholipids was needed to reveal the vesicle intermediate.

surprise.text: I was surprised that membrane growth required phospholipids and proteins to form vesicles first, rather than adding phospholipids directly to the cell.

arbitrary.text: The initial direct growth attempt felt arbitrary because the cell had no available combination, although the subsequent vesicle construction gave the route a clearer purpose.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: the constructions made the distinct stages of cell division understandable, and the ending raises the question of how cells with the same genome become different through gene expression.
